analysis.one_liner: Directs the FDA to set enforceable limits on toxic heavy metals in baby food and juice.
analysis.headline: The Baby Food Safety Act of 2024 never got a vote: introduced in May 2024 with 2 cosponsors, it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the FDA to set legal limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in food made for babies and toddlers, in fruit and vegetable puree pouches, and in juice. Companies making these foods would have to test their finished products at accredited labs, keep records, run environmental monitoring in their plants, and could face mandatory recalls if contaminated products reach shelves. It was introduced in May 2024, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Babies, toddlers, and their parents. The bill targets contaminants like lead and arsenic that build up in young children's bodies and can harm brain development, and it would give the FDA power to force recalls of contaminated baby food rather than relying on companies to voluntarily pull it.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to set enforceable limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in infant and toddler food, puree pouches, and juice, with deadlines starting at the end of 2025 [S2].
Makes food adulterated — illegal to sell — if it exceeds those limits or if its maker fails the required testing and recordkeeping [S2].
Requires makers of baby food to sample and test finished products at internationally accredited labs, keep two years of records, and submit to FDA verification testing [S2].
Gives the FDA mandatory recall authority over contaminated infant and toddler food, which it does not have today [S2].
Requires environmental monitoring for pathogens and heavy metals inside baby food plants [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Baby food and juice manufacturers, who would bear the cost of lab testing, environmental monitoring, recordkeeping, and reformulating products to meet the new limits. Some of that cost would likely show up on store shelves.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for testing, monitoring, and reformulation would fall on baby food and juice makers and could be passed to families through higher prices [S2].

The bill preempts states from setting their own, potentially stricter contaminant limits or labeling requirements for these foods, replacing a patchwork with a single federal standard that could be weaker than what some states would adopt [S2].
The deadlines are slow: cadmium limits were not due until 2026 and mercury limits until 2028, and testing requirements would not start until two years after enactment [S2].
In setting limits, the FDA must account for contaminants that 'cannot be avoided' in production, which gives the agency room to set thresholds above zero [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is real: babies are especially vulnerable to heavy metals, and today there are no binding federal limits for most of these foods and no mandatory recall authority. The costs are testing and reformulation expenses for a small set of manufacturers, plus the loss of state-level rules that could have gone further or faster. On balance it is a straightforward safety regulation, though its slow timelines and preemption of state rules blunt the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2024 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and the bill died when Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the Baby Food Safety Act of 2024 in the House on May 14, 2024 [S1][S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and to the subcommittee on Health on May 17, 2024 [S4].
The bill attracted only 2 cosponsors, both Democrats [S3].
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Baby food and juice manufacturers avoided new federal testing requirements, contaminant limits, and mandatory recall exposure. Parents gained no binding federal limits on heavy metals in baby food.

for.name: Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing or markup before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough to produce votes or recorded opposition; it was sponsored and cosponsored only by Democrats, and the Republican-led committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill would impose binding contaminant limits, accredited-lab testing, plant monitoring, and mandatory recall exposure on infant and toddler food makers, who currently face no binding federal heavy-metal limits for these products. Lower contaminant levels for children come directly at these companies' compliance and reformulation expense.

industries.industry: Fruit and vegetable puree pouch and juice processors
industries.note: The bill extends the same contaminant limits, sampling, and testing requirements to puree pouches and juice, requiring compliance programs and accredited-lab testing. The public health gain is borne as a cost by these processors.
